#81980. CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1456 w)

CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1456 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles.
  • Recent findings suggest that the evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
  • Recent findings suggest that the elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The long-awaited result could help scientists investigate a largely unexplored realm of physics where unknown particles and forces of nature may exist.

Recent findings suggest that the evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester played notable roles in the international effort, contributing to the advanced technology that made the measurement possible.

Recent findings suggest that the elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That is strong enough to qualify as evidence, but physicists will need additional data before they can officially declare a discovery. Even so, the finding marks a major milestone in a search that has lasted more than 40 years.

It also creates upcoming opportunities to test the Standard Model, the leading scientific framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact. By examining this exceptionally rare decay in greater detail, researchers hope to uncover subtle clues that could eventually point toward physics beyond our current understanding.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal Fresh Physics.

The LHCb experiment specializes in studying particles that contain beauty quarks. These are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of the ordinary matter around us.

When particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider, enormous numbers of beauty quarks are produced. However, they survive for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying into other particles.

Scientists study these transformations because they may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider. By measuring exactly how frequently different decays occur, physicists can search for unexpected effects that might indicate previously unknown physics.

It has been revealed that particularly rare decays offer an important advantage. Because they happen so infrequently, their rates can be especially sensitive to contributions from undiscovered particles. Even small differences between predicted and observed decay rates could provide valuable evidence of newly introduced forces or particles.

A One in 10 Billion Particle Decay.

The newly observed signal involves a process known as 'Bd to mu mu'. During this decay, a particle containing a beauty quark transforms into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons.

According to theoretical predictions, this transformation should occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. Despite decades of investigation, no individual experiment had previously produced convincing evidence that it occurs.

Industry observers note that the upgraded LHCb experiment has now achieved a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. Although this meets the standard for reporting evidence, particle physicists generally require a significance of five sigma before announcing a confirmed discovery.

Industry observers note that professor Chris Parkes, Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration during construction of its major upgrade. He also oversaw the collaboration's approval of the new findings.

He explained: "The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking -- a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

Sources indicate that "The UK made the largest national contribution to the project, pioneering newly introduced technologies that have made today's result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start; we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale.".

Parkes, who became a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year in recognition of his contributions to LHCb, offered a memorable comparison to illustrate just how improbable the decay is.

"This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth.".

Advanced LHC Detectors Make the Breakthrough Possible.

Detecting such an uncommon event requires instruments capable of following the movements of particles with extraordinary accuracy.

One of the most important components of the upgraded LHCb experiment is a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from researchers in the United Kingdom. Called the Vertex Locator, it measures the paths of particles generated during collisions inside the collider.

Positioned just five millimeters from the LHC beams, the detector allows researchers to determine precisely where particles originate and where they subsequently decay.

Dr. Stefano De Capua, who directed detector construction at the University of Manchester, described the extensive collaboration behind the technology.

It has been revealed that "We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons.".

The wider LHCb upgrade also allows the experiment to gather information at up to five times its previous rate. This greater capacity, together with improvements in tracking technology, is helping physicists identify events that were previously too difficult to measure reliably.

Exploring the Mysterious Zeptoverse.

Beyond confirming an exceptionally rare particle process, the result could help scientists investigate what they call the 'Zeptoverse'.

Sources indicate that this name refers to an almost unimaginably small scale, measured in zeptometers. A single zeptometer is just a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. Physicists suspect that effects from currently unknown particles and forces could become apparent when nature is examined at these extreme scales.

Sources indicate that for now, the new measurement agrees with the Standard Model. Researchers have not found evidence that the established theory is wrong, but increasingly precise measurements could reveal deviations that current experiments cannot yet detect.

Such differences would be especially significant because they could indicate where the Standard Model stops providing a complete explanation of the physical world.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, who serves as Deputy Physics Coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, emphasized the importance of finally obtaining the long-sought signal.

Recent findings suggest that "There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of latest physics from beyond our current knowledge.

"The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.".

What Comes Next for CERN's Particle Research?

The upgraded LHCb experiment is expected to continue gathering a substantially larger collection of measurements into the early 2030s. With more data, physicists should be able to determine the frequency of this rare decay with much greater precision.

According to recent reports, researchers are also planning another major upgrade that could increase data collection rates by an additional factor of ten. This would improve their ability to investigate extremely rare particle processes and search for the effects of unknown particles at even smaller distance scales.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who did not participate in the experiment, highlighted how improvements in scientific instruments can lead to notable advances in understanding nature.

It has been revealed that "This is an vital result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments, and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don't understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing -- that's science! LHCb is a major scientific success.".

The experiment receives funding from the Science and Technology Facilities Council, which operates within UK Research and Innovation. The UK LHCb collaboration brings together scientists from ten universities across the United Kingdom and the STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory.

Although the newly detected decay has not yet revealed any unknown particles or forces, it gives physicists a powerful upcoming way to search for them. After more than 40 years of effort, an extraordinarily elusive process is finally becoming accessible to detailed study, potentially bringing researchers closer to understanding some of the universe's deepest mysteries.

#81979. Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1939 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million people a month.
  • But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.
  • While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million people a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

It has been revealed that multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Firm insiders said the exploits were utilized to spy on consumers and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” said Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

The revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational tech giant with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

In a recent development, there is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any tech giant operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg said a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”.

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Recent findings suggest that pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly owners until the end of 2018, the year it listed in Upcoming York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the tech giant set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the company only targeted users in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they said.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the company was able to create a comprehensive portrait of consumers’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting users to open the app and place orders, they said.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

Google Play is not available in China, and Android people in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it remarked it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” said Hyppönen.

It has been revealed that the app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen mentioned. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers said.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they noted.

According to recent reports, in China, about three quarters of smartphone users are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, said Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

“I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he said.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

Toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.

Pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he said.

Industry observers note that according to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to users’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he noted.

According to recent reports, of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews indicated that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” noted René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

Industry observers note that suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread quickly among other researchers, who did name the tech giant. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a newly introduced update of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the update, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

In a recent development, the next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the company’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to big data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source mentioned.

It has been revealed that most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the upgrade, noted although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Major Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology released a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

In 2021, Beijing passed its first comprehensive data privacy legislation.

The Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” said Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”.

Industry observers note that the ministry has regularly published lists to name and shame apps found to have undermined user privacy or other rights. It also publishes a separate list of apps that are removed from app stores for failing to comply with regulations.

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

Industry observers note that “Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

The post was censored the next day.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.
  • In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.
  • Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.

In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.

Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure.".

The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.

Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

Recent findings suggest that "We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot.".

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation.".

In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

It has been revealed that many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.

Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.

Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he stated was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.

"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.

Sources indicate that china's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.

Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security.".

PwC noted Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those latest technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.

"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.

With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

Recent findings suggest that wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.

"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.

Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

In a recent development, domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).

IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

In a recent development, in Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000.".

Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.

For Germany, the issue isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany.".

"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

Latest Update: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1250 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most notable genes by making them less likely to mutate?
  • In a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr.
  • The findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most notable genes by making them less likely to mutate? First proposed in 1972, the hypothesis challenges the traditional understanding of how genetic changes arise. Now, new research from the University of Bath suggests that the evidence supporting this idea has been misleading.

In a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr. Sofia Radrizzani and Professor Laurence D Hurst of the University of Bath's Centre for Evolution examined the largest collection of spontaneous genetic mutations assembled to date. Their analysis focused on two microorganisms: the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli) and the single-celled fungus baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).

The findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival. Although this theory has repeatedly attracted scientific attention since its introduction, including a renewed debate in 2023, the researchers say their results undermine its central premise.

In a recent development, "The claim that mutation is slower for key genes is a triumph of hype over substance," remarked Dr. Radrizzani, who co-wrote the new paper as part of her PhD. "It's a really old suggestion and is reinvented in various forms routinely.".

How Mutations and Natural Selection Drive Evolution.

It has been revealed that the conventional explanation of evolution involves two main processes. Genetic mutations first introduce variation among organisms. Natural selection then influences which of those variations become more common, favoring traits that improve survival and reproduction. This process can be compared to a sieve that separates different kinds of material, allowing some genetic changes to persist while others disappear.

A familiar example comes from Darwin's finches, which Charles Darwin first encountered on the Galápagos Islands in 1835. These birds have different beak shapes that help them feed on different foods. Random mutations contribute to variations in beak size and shape, and when certain food sources become more plentiful, birds with better-suited beaks are more likely to survive and reproduce. Over many generations, these advantageous traits can spread through the population.

In a recent development, however, an alternative hypothesis suggests that mutations may not occur as randomly as the conventional model assumes. According to this idea, organisms have evolved ways to reduce mutations in their most critical genes (such as those involved in replicating DNA or maintaining basic cellular machinery). Meanwhile, genes in which changes might provide useful adaptations (such as those in which mutations give bacteria resistance to antibiotics, or change beak dimensions) could experience higher mutation rates.

Sources indicate that at first glance, protecting essential genes seems like an obvious evolutionary advantage. Mutations affecting these genes can disrupt vital biological processes, cause genetic diseases, or even kill an organism. If such changes are so dangerous, why wouldn't natural selection favor mechanisms that prevent them?

The problem, researchers explain, is that mutations in individual genes are already relatively rare. Reducing those rates even further would provide only a tiny additional benefit, making it difficult for natural selection to favor such a protective system.

The Mystery of Disappearing Genetic Mutations.

Another problem lies in how scientists have measured mutations in earlier research. Notable genes may appear to mutate less frequently not because they are better protected, but because harmful mutations in those genes are swiftly eliminated from populations.

Professor Hurst noted: "We'd expect natural selection to rapidly remove mutations when they occur in more key genes, because these mutations are more likely to be harmful to the organism. This can create the illusion that important genes have fewer mutations when, in reality, some mutations have simply disappeared before we have a chance to analyze them - what you can think of as 'ghost mutations'.".

This distinction is crucial. When scientists examine the genetic changes remaining in a population, they may miss mutations that occurred but were subsequently removed by natural selection. As a result, the apparent stability of essential genes could reflect the disappearance of damaging mutations rather than a lower likelihood of those mutations occurring in the first place.

A Major Test of the 50-Year-Old Evolutionary Theory.

According to recent reports, to investigate the question more directly, the University of Bath team analyzed data from experiments designed to record mutations while minimizing the influence of natural selection. These experiments, known as mutation accumulation studies, allowed researchers to examine genetic changes in E. coli and baker's yeast without the usual strong filtering effects of selection.

Recent findings suggest that the scientists also performed three independent tests to determine whether natural selection might still have significantly distorted the data. None revealed evidence of substantial bias.

Dr. Radrizzani said: "This looks like the largest and cleanest sample of mutations assembled to date.".

With this extensive dataset, the researchers investigated whether genes that are more crucial for survival actually experience fewer mutations.

They assessed gene importance using experiments in which individual genes were removed from organisms. Some genes are indispensable, meaning that cells die without them. Others can be deleted with little or no noticeable effect.

Sources indicate that if the protective mutation hypothesis were correct, the most essential genes should have shown consistently lower mutation rates. Instead, the researchers found no such relationship in either microorganism.

Professor Hurst said: "Analyze the data any which way and we found nothing. In neither species did these key genes have a lower mutation rate.".

What Really Determines How Often Genes Mutate?

The team also examined whether other measures of gene importance could explain differences in mutation rates. These included the amount of protein produced by each gene and how strongly natural selection had shaped genes over thousands of years.

Once again, the results failed to support the idea that more notable genes receive special protection.

Dr. Radrizzani said: "We found that genes producing more abundant proteins don't have lower mutation rates. Nor does the way genes evolve over thousands of years predict how frequently they mutate.".

It has been revealed that that does not mean every gene has exactly the same chance of mutating. The researchers identified features of genome structure and DNA replication that influence mutation frequency. For example, genes copied later during DNA replication tend to accumulate mutations more frequently than those copied earlier.

These findings indicate that mutation rates can vary across the genome, but the differences do not appear to reflect a system that specifically shields essential genes from genetic changes.

Industry observers note that professor Hurst said: "While we see known causes of variation in mutation rates, we found no evidence for the effects that have been proposed as a challenge to the conventional model. None predicted which genes would have high or low mutation rates, and there are certainly no grounds for a shift in paradigm.".

Industry observers note that the research therefore provides latest support for the conventional distinction between mutation and natural selection. Although mutations do not occur at identical rates everywhere in the genome, the evidence from bacteria and yeast offers no indication that evolution systematically protects its most notable genes by reducing how often they mutate.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that even as the unusually quiet 2026 storm season winds down in the North Atlantic, seas have begun to stir on the other side of the world in the Southwest Pacific.
  • Sources indicate that named Xavier, the system intensified rapidly, thriving in an environment with minimal wind shear and sea surface temperatures of 29 degrees Celsius (84 degrees Fahrenheit)—well above the threshold required to sustain and strengthen developing tropical cyclones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tropical Cyclone Xavier rolled out the basin’s storm season with a bang.

It has been revealed that even as the unusually quiet 2026 storm season winds down in the North Atlantic, seas have begun to stir on the other side of the world in the Southwest Pacific. On November 15, 2026, the Fiji Meteorological Service began issuing updates about a slow-moving tropical disturbance northeast of Samoa and the Cook Islands. Within just a few days, it had become one of the most intense November tropical cyclones the region has seen in decades.

Sources indicate that named Xavier, the system intensified rapidly, thriving in an environment with minimal wind shear and sea surface temperatures of 29 degrees Celsius (84 degrees Fahrenheit)—well above the threshold required to sustain and strengthen developing tropical cyclones. Xavier was the basin’s second named storm of the season, following only Wati, a short-lived storm that emerged in October.

As Xavier developed, NASA satellite data showed the storm churning along the southwestern edge of a massive tongue of warm water spanning from the west coast of South America to the central Pacific—a telltale sign of the El Niño that has been present in the region since June.

When the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Aqua satellite captured this image at 02:53 Universal Time on November 17, 2026 (4:53 p.m. Cook Islands Time on November 16), forecasters estimated Xavier had maximum winds of about 195 kilometers (120 miles) per hour. Winds reached a peak intensity of 220 kilometers (140 miles) per hour later that day, a Category 5 storm on the cyclone intensity scale used in the region or a Category 4 on the Saffir-Simpson scale.

The storm ranks as the strongest November tropical cyclone east of the international date line on record, noted Colorado State University hurricane expert Phil Klotzbach. Xavier’s formation east of the date line, near the northern Cook Islands, was unusual, but its easterly position aligns with research that indicates that storm activity in the region typically shifts northeast during El Niño years. Research also demonstrates that El Niño tends to fuel storms that strengthen at an unusually rapid pace.

According to news reports, Xavier damaged homes and caused power disruptions as it passed the northern Cook Islands. It then encountered dry air and a less favorable wind shear environment and slowly weakened as it pushed westward, reducing the threat that it posed to Samoa and American Samoa.

In a recent development, xavier is likely one of the first of several storms to affect the region in the coming months. A seasonal outlook from the Fiji Meteorological Service projects that the region could see between 11 and 15 named tropical cyclones this season, with the greatest risk east of the international date line. Storm activity in the Southwest Pacific basin typically peaks in February.

It has been revealed that explanation: On November 17, fans of interstellar spaceflight around planet Earth were invited to shine a message into the night sky. Traced by a flashlight beam switched on and off, the dashes and dots of a Morse code message captured in this time exposure from the Emirates Astronomical Observatory are read V-G-R. That's a call sign for the Voyager 1 spacecraft at the moment in interstellar space some 26 billion kilometers away. How long did it take the message to reach humanity's most distant interstellar spacecraft? Traveling at the speed of light, the answer is one day. In fact, the Voyager 1 spacecraft was confirmed to reach its one light-day distance milestone on November 18, at 10:16:07 UTC, nearly 50 years after launch in 1977. Latest Update: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means.
  • The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations.
  • "What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," says Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means. Latest research reveals that scientists disagree about the nature and purpose of science even more than the general public does.

The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations. Even when scientists generally supported a particular definition, many questioned some aspect of it.

"What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," says Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.

It has been revealed that members of the public, by comparison, expressed more consistent views. They were more likely to regard science as a dependable way to discover objective truths about the world, placing less importance on the uncertainty and creativity involved in scientific research.

According to recent reports, these contrasting perspectives may have crucial consequences. They could affect the questions scientists choose to investigate and influence how people evaluate scientific findings. They may also help explain why the public sometimes becomes frustrated when researchers cannot offer clear answers or change their conclusions in response to new evidence.

What Scientists and the Public Believe About Science.

Sources indicate that dubova, now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, worked with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu to investigate how people understand science.

According to recent reports, the researchers surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants were asked to assess 18 descriptions of science drawn from historical perspectives, including comparisons of scientific research to detective work, a pursuit of truth, and a mirror that reflects reality.

Recent findings suggest that both groups generally agreed that curiosity, exploration, and the desire to solve mysteries are central to science. Beyond those shared ideas, however, the scientists expressed strikingly different perspectives.

In a recent development, some researchers viewed science primarily as a means of discovering objective truths. Others placed greater importance on imagination, personal judgment, and the creative decisions involved in research. Scientists also differed over whether scientific progress depends mainly on following established procedures or adapting and improvising as new challenges arise.

It has been revealed that dubova believes these disagreements may reflect the individual experiences that shape how researchers approach their work. Just as chefs can have very different philosophies about preparing food, scientists can develop distinct ideas about the best ways to investigate the world.

Why the Public Sees Science Differently.

It has been revealed that another intriguing finding involved differences among scientific disciplines. The general public's understanding of science more closely resembled the views expressed by physicists and biologists than those of psychologists and other social scientists.

One possible reason is that physics and biology receive greater attention in science education, potentially shaping how people imagine scientific research. Dubova emphasizes, however, that this explanation remains tentative and will require additional investigation.

Industry observers note that the differences between scientists and the public could also help explain misunderstandings about scientific uncertainty. People who expect science to produce firm, objective answers may have difficulty understanding why findings sometimes conflict or why scientific conclusions must be updated when upcoming evidence becomes available.

What the Findings Could Mean for AI and Scientific Discovery.

The research also points to a potential challenge as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly involved in scientific discovery.

With researchers developing AI systems that can carry out scientific investigations, Dubova is concerned that automation could favor a limited conception of how science should work. If those systems are built around one particular approach to research, other valuable methods of discovery could receive less attention.

The study received support from the Santa Fe Institute's Lou Schuyler Seed Grant Fund, which was created in 2022 to encourage exploratory projects by early career scientists. Dubova used the funding to pay participants for taking part in the research.

For Dubova, the findings represent an initial effort to understand how scientists' underlying beliefs about their profession might influence the research they conduct and the discoveries they make.

According to recent reports, "Don't take the common understanding of science for granted," she indicates. "Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind.".

Thank the gods, Percy Jackson remembered it should be funny

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disney+'s Percy Jackson and the Olympians series has done an admirable job of adapting the Greek mythology-inspired adventures of Rick Riordan's novels.
  • The book series are narrated by Percy Jackson (Walker Scobell) himself, whose internal monologue contains its fair range of sass and hilariously deadpan descriptions of the strange things that happen to him.
  • It has been revealed that the TV series borrows these chapter headings for its own episode titles, but loses a significant chunk of the humor that make them land on the page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disney+'s Percy Jackson and the Olympians series has done an admirable job of adapting the Greek mythology-inspired adventures of Rick Riordan's novels. But it has consistently struggled with a key aspect of of the books: their humor.

The book series are narrated by Percy Jackson (Walker Scobell) himself, whose internal monologue contains its fair range of sass and hilariously deadpan descriptions of the strange things that happen to him. Case in point, every book's irreverent chapter titles, which kick off with the iconic "I Accidentally Vaporize My Pre-Algebra Teacher" and go on to include such hits as "I Battle My Jerk Relative" and "Everybody Hates Me but the Horse.".

It has been revealed that the TV series borrows these chapter headings for its own episode titles, but loses a significant chunk of the humor that make them land on the page. It sands down much of the wisecracking banter between Percy and his questing companions, turning them into more stoic fantasy heroes. Yes, Season 2 features one of the books' funniest moments: the fan-favorite scene of Grover (Aryan Simhadri) wearing a wedding dress to escape from cyclops Polyphemus. (It throws Percy in a dress too for good measure.) But it also misses out on the smaller wordplay or misunderstandings that drew major laughs from the books, like when Percy mistakes the word "hubris" for "hummus." It's a solid joke, as well as a reminder that Percy is just a kid caught in the crossfires of a mythic war. In missing out on these gags, small as they may be, the show has failed to let Percy and his companions be kids, and also struggled to capture the books' distinct tone.

Thankfully, the first two episodes of Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3 prove to be a refreshing change of pace, right from their very first moments. The season begins with a tense monster fight for Thalia (Tamara Smart), during which Percy intervenes and helps her kills her foe. When she tells him she had everything under control, a car bursts into flames in the background.

In a recent development, it's a classic gag, one that by no means reinvents the wheel. But it gets better when Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries) asks Percy to put out the fire. As she and Thalia have a serious chat, we see him exasperatedly playing firefighter in the background. Here is a perfect example of how to balance the Percy Jackson and the Olympians books' high stakes with humor, and the TV series keeps it up from there.

It has been revealed that turns out, the key to unlocking Percy Jackson's comic potential is the contentious relationship between Percy and Thalia. The pair butt heads throughout the first two episodes, over everything from how to deal with Kronos ally Luke (Charlie Bushnell) to undertaking a quest. There's real dramatic tension there, but Percy Jackson and the Olympians emphasizes it with a running undercurrent of sassy snapping. When Thalia mentions her dream of battling Percy to the death, she wonders if it will come true.

"No!" Percy notes, affronted. Then, as a follow-up beat, he asks, "Who won?".

In addition to the often sarcastic back-and-forth between Percy and Thalia, Percy Jackson and the Olympians finds other ways to levels up its humor. Its fight scenes get the occasional jolt of laughter, like when Annabeth orders Grover to "goat kick" a foe. The show also leans further into the kinds of descriptions Percy would give in his internal monologue in the books. When he sets foot in the imposing military academy of Westover, he remarks it looks like students are "training for Dracula's army." That's not a line that's actually in The Titan's Curse (Percy likens it to "an evil knight's castle" instead), yet it feels like it could be ripped straight from its pages.

Elsewhere, the series finds genuinely funny ways to cut its intense storyline. After Annabeth reminds Percy he said he'd burn down Olympus to save her, he utters a hapless, "I was having a bad day when I said that." A later scene involving Percy and Thalia waiting for a prophecy from the Oracle also left me in stitches. Who other than Percy Jackson would ask a mummified Oracle for a high five in the hopes of waking her up?

It has been revealed that even the gods are funnier this season. Apollo (Hubert Smielecki) being a hot-shot bro who jams out to "Walking on Sunshine" contrasts perfectly with his sister, fierce huntress Artemis (Dafne Keen). Hearing her snarl "We are twins" after he keeps calling her "kid sis" is exactly the level of petty family drama I want to see from the Olympians.

Industry observers note that none of this increased humor detracts from Percy Jackson and the Olympians' dramatic stakes. Far from it! The dark moments — and book readers know that this season will get dark — still land, even more so now that they've been juxtaposed with genuine lightness. Like in the books, that lightness emphasizes just how young these characters are, which makes their brutal trials even more heartbreaking. And with The Titan's Curse's fan-favorite "dam" jokes on the way, confirmed by Scobell himself, we know we'll be in for a lot more humor combined with that heartbreak.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Engineers and analysts searching for the root cause of the technical issues behind Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration have been able to replicate the situation that was overwhelming parts of the air traffic system, people familiar with the investigation told CNBC.

According to recent reports, while replicating the glitch in a lab in Florida is progress, those investigating the matter have yet to determine exactly why two routers in question failed, according to the people, who requested anonymity to talk about an ongoing situation. Finding the root cause is critical to the FAA determining if there may be an issue with other routers that form the backbone of communications for the national air transportation network.

Sources indicate that the ground stop lasted for more than four hours Friday, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have said there is no indication the routers failed due to a cyberattack.

The incident in question happened shortly after L3Harris Technologies, the primary contractor supporting the FAA telecommunications network, installed a new router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas.

L3Harris noted that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.

Recent findings suggest that "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement stated. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.".

Investigators remarked within eight minutes of its installation, the router began to transmit too much data within the FAA network.

That surge of data, 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds, Duffy said.

In a recent development, since the ground stop, Duffy has increased the amount of money he wants to upgrade the national air traffic system. After originally asking for $30 billion to build a digital network that will incorporate artificial intelligence, Duffy has now asked Congress for $50 billion.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that to his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light. Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast.

In a recent development, rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io. He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years.

It has been revealed that to his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule.

Rømer figured out the pattern and made an accurate prediction for Io's eclipse on Nov. 9, 1676. Then on Nov. 21, he took his findings to the Royal Academy of Sciences and explained that a finite speed of light must be responsible.

According to recent reports, understanding that the speed of light is a constant is the key that opened our ability to gauge the scale of the universe, as well as was central to developing modern physics."The speed of light becomes a sort of ultimate speed limit," Live Science explained in an article about why the speed of light matters. "In fact, objects with mass, be they cars or neutrinos, can't reach the speed of light because they would need infinite energy to do so.".

On this day in space! Nov. 20, 1998: Russia introduces 1st module of International Space Station as construction begins on the largest human-built structure in orbit.

After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She at the moment lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training.
  • Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on concerns that matter to them, such as climate protection.
  • In a recent development, what particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a massive city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on concerns that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

In a recent development, what particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today.".

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," claims Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests.".

The 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

According to recent reports, UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30.".

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," notes Brod.

Industry observers note that he is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an key step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

According to recent reports, sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

In a recent development, her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have noted 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!".

#81961. Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1102 w)

Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1102 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.
  • The limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD.
  • It has been revealed that now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.

The limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD. However, a large Latin cross carved into its lid dates to approximately the 10th or 11th century, suggesting that the person buried inside lived hundreds of years after the coffin was originally made.

It has been revealed that now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation. The remains likely belong to a prominent medieval monk, and researchers have narrowed the possible identities to two men who once led Westminster Abbey.

Two Medieval Abbots Emerge as Leading Candidates.

The latest findings, published in the peer-reviewed Journal of the British Archaeological Association, come from Professor Warwick Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

Recent findings suggest that rodwell identifies Aelfwig, an abbot who died around 1020, as the strongest candidate. At the time, Westminster Abbey was a Benedictine monastery, and Aelfwig had served there as a monk before becoming its abbot.

Industry observers note that another possibility is Wulnoth, who succeeded Aelfwig and died in 1049. Both men are believed to have been buried at the Abbey, making either a plausible match for the skeleton.

"We have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus," says Professor Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

Sources indicate that "We do not know the date of birth of either. But either would fit equally well if we assume the Abbot was in his early twenties when the appointment was made and close to fifty when he died.

"The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.".

The elaborate burial provides another reason to suspect that the deceased held an notable position. Rodwell suggests that the individual was 'honored' with a 'fine sarcophagus', an unusual distinction that would be consistent with the status of an abbot.

It has been revealed that rather than commissioning an entirely new stone coffin, those responsible for the burial apparently reused an existing Roman sarcophagus. The man's wooden coffin was placed inside it, and the stone lid was modified with a prominent Latin cross. This may represent an early example of recycling a valuable object for an entirely different purpose.

New Excavations Reveal the Skeleton's Age.

In a recent development, the Roman sarcophagus and its mysterious occupant have fascinated researchers for generations. Rodwell's latest conclusions draw on several investigations conducted with specialists over the years, including work associated with Channel 4's Time Team.

In 2009, the television program examined the archaeology and architecture of King Henry III's original sacristy, located along the north side of Westminster Abbey.

The same area was the scene of an earlier accidental discovery in 1820, when workers encountered the Roman coffin and broke its lid into six pieces. The damage was repaired around the time the sarcophagus was formally 'discovered' in 1869.

Recent findings suggest that more recently, Pre-Construct Archaeology, one of the UK's largest commercial archaeological and heritage organizations, carried out another excavation of the sacristy. Completed in 2025, the project was undertaken to support construction of the King Charles III Sacristy, a upcoming facility at Westminster Abbey scheduled to open the following year.

As part of this investigation, human bone specialist James Young Langthorne of Pre-Construct Archaeology (PCA) conducted a fresh examination of the skeleton.

According to recent reports, his analysis indicated that the deceased was a man between 35 and 49 years old who stood approximately 5 feet 9 inches tall. These findings differ considerably from an assessment made in the 1800s, which described the remains as those of a 'robust young man' no older than 30 and approximately 5 feet 7 inches tall.

Carbon Dating Confirms a 1,000-Year-Old Burial.

One of the most vital clues came from scientific dating of the remains. A bone sample was submitted to the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre for radiocarbon analysis, which produced a date range of 987 to 1052 AD.

It has been revealed that this places the burial firmly within the late Saxon period, centuries after the Roman sarcophagus was originally created. The dates also align with the deaths of both Aelfwig and Wulnoth, strengthening the case that the skeleton belonged to one of these medieval abbots.

"This confirms that the reuse of the sarcophagus, and the associated remodeling of its cover, occurred in the late Saxon period.".

The results provide scientific support for the theory that an ancient Roman burial container was repurposed to honor an important religious figure nearly 1,000 years ago.

A Skeleton Thought Lost Was Hiding in Plain Sight.

The investigation also brought renewed attention to an unexpected discovery made in 2016. For years, researchers had believed that the skeleton was missing, leaving an key part of the burial's history unresolved.

That assumption proved mistaken when the sarcophagus was transported to a conservation studio. PCA researchers removed its lid and were surprised to find an almost complete human skeleton still inside.

In a recent development, the examination produced another clue that Rodwell describes as a 'remarkable upcoming discovery'. Inside the stone coffin, researchers identified the rectangular outline of a structure that had disappeared long ago. Its shape was preserved by a white residue left behind by lime, a material historically used in burials.

Rodwell believes the outline marks the position of the original wooden coffin that held the deceased before it was placed inside the Roman sarcophagus.

"Although no physical traces of that feature remained, it can only have been a timber coffin, which has completely decayed over the course of the seven centuries that the sarcophagus was buried in the sacristy courtyard," writes Professor Rodwell.

Together, the rediscovered skeleton, evidence of a wooden coffin, and upcoming scientific dating have transformed researchers' understanding of this unusual burial. Although the man's identity has not been established beyond doubt, the findings suggest that a medieval abbot may have been laid to rest in a Roman coffin already centuries old.

Visitors can see the sarcophagus today in the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries at Westminster Abbey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that employees contributing to NASA’s mission at the agency’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, were recognized during the center’s Honor Awards ceremony on Nov. 18.

Presenting the awards were Christine Powell, NASA Stennis center director, and Jeremy Parsons, the agency’s Artemis program manager responsible for management and oversight of NASA’s initiative to return humans to the Moon.

Stephen Rawls of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Center Director’s Excellence Award for exceptional leadership and technical excellence in advancing NASA Stennis propulsion testing capabilities for critical NASA and commercial programs.

Bradley Tyree of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Engineering Excellence Award for engineering excellence and contributions to the successful testing of the Liquid Oxygen/Liquid Methane Assessment Confined by Missile Program.

Anna Lizana of Diamondhead, Mississippi, received the Excellence in Customer Service Award for exceptional environmental compliance support that advanced commercial partnerships, streamlined agency processes, and reduced regulatory risk.

Daniel Jones of Huntsville, Alabama, received the Excellence in Innovation Award for the invention of the Hydrocarbon Propellants Enabling Reproduction of Flows in Rocket Engines, a system for low-cost aerodynamic data acquisition.

Peyton Pinson of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Leadership Excellence Award for exceptional leadership as E-1 test director, providing steady guidance and strengthening team cohesion throughout a demanding and high-tempo year of propulsion testing.

Recent findings suggest that joseph Schuyler of Pass Christian, Mississippi, received the J. Harry Guin Leadership Award for transformative leadership that advanced NASA Stennis propulsion testing capability and strengthened its role as the agency’s Center of Excellence in Propulsion Testing.

According to recent reports, michael McDaniel of Slidell, Louisiana, received the Roy S. Estess Service Leadership Award for exceptional partnership, sustained leadership, and an unwavering commitment to his community as the general manager of L3Harris Technologies at NASA Stennis that embodies the legacy of the late center director.

Amer Arshad of Diamondhead, Mississippi, received the Space Flight Awareness Trailblazer Award for innovative leadership, system stewardship, and collaborative solutions that have strengthened NASA’s mission through improved reliability, insight, and efficiency.

Claire O’Shaughnessy of Mandeville, Louisiana, received the Space Flight Awareness Trailblazer Award for innovative leadership and collaborative drive that strengthened the center’s mission by advancing critical facility capabilities for the agency’s Artemis program.

In a recent development, in addition to individual awards, the Liquid Oxygen/Liquid Methane Assessment, Confined by Missile Test Team received the Space Flight Awareness Team Award for exceptional technical achievement in executing a test series that has provided mission critical safety data for the future of human spaceflight. Briou Bourgeois accepted the award on behalf of the team, which included: Chase Aubry, Brandon Carver, Jack Conley, James Connell, Armando Delgado, Mateo Ferreira, Pau Fuller, Mark Hancock, Steven Helmstetter, Paula Hensarling, Jason Hopper, Chase Lemaire, Addison Mitchell, Randall Pigott, Stephen Rawls, Skip Roberts, Mark Robinson, Luke Roger, Matthew Sappington, Robert Simmers, Jason Richard, Bradley Tyree, Richard Wear, and Robert Williams.

Recent findings suggest that the ceremony also honored employees who reached significant milestone anniversaries in their civil service careers. Employees with 40 years of service were Curtis Armstrong, Jason Edge, and Kevin Power. Employees with 35 years of service were Michael Brashear, Reginald Ellis II, Arlen Griffey, Bradley Messer, Christine Powell, and Michael Rewis. Skip Roberts was recognized for 30 years of service. Employees with 25 years of service were Gregory Carmouche, Thomas Carroll, Craig Chandler, Jorge Figueroa, Jared Grover, Melissa Huggins, Scott Jensen, Jeffrey Lott, Christopher Mulkey, Richard Rauch, Ryan Roberts, Karen Seals, Joseph Schuyler, Peterve Tran, and Maury Vander.
