#81957. Industry News: Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (927 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.
  • Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.
  • The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

Recent findings suggest that the east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

But now there has been a breakthrough.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Sources indicate that brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle.".

Recent findings suggest that only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

In a recent development, then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!".

Recent findings suggest that nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Sources indicate that brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go.".

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another important discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

Recent findings suggest that using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

It has been revealed that there is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

Greece, however, considers them stolen.

For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

Sources indicate that the exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

This article was originally written in German.

Latest Update: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, newly introduced observations and computer simulations have revealed a surprising possible source of mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole.
  • According to recent reports, the center of our galaxy is an extraordinarily crowded and active environment.
  • Over the past two decades, infrared observations have revealed several small, dense gas clouds traveling close to Sagittarius A*.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, newly introduced observations and computer simulations have revealed a surprising possible source of mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole. An international research team led by MPE has traced these compact clouds to a massive pair of stars whose powerful winds appear to produce material that could eventually help feed the black hole, known as Sagittarius A*.

According to recent reports, the center of our galaxy is an extraordinarily crowded and active environment. At its core sits Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), a supermassive black hole surrounded by stars, gas, and dust moving through a region dominated by intense gravitational forces. This extreme setting gives astronomers an opportunity to investigate how matter moves near black holes and where the material that sustains their activity comes from.

Over the past two decades, infrared observations have revealed several small, dense gas clouds traveling close to Sagittarius A*. These mysterious "clumps" may provide key clues about how material makes its way toward the black hole. However, scientists have struggled to determine where the clouds originate and what causes them to form.

Mysterious Gas Clouds Near the Milky Way's Black Hole.

In a recent development, one of the first major discoveries came in 2012, when astronomers identified a compact cloud of ionized gas called G2. Containing several times Earth's mass, the cloud produces emissions from hydrogen and helium, consistent with hot gas mixed with dust. It follows a highly elongated orbit around Sagittarius A* and has a faint extension trailing behind it, known as G2t.

Soon afterward, researchers examining older observations recognized another similar object, G1, traveling along a closely related path. The similarities suggested that G1, G2, and G2t might not be independent objects. Instead, they could represent concentrations of gas within a larger, continuous stream.

Even relatively small differences in gas density can make such a stream appear broken into separate clouds. This happens because the brightness of the gas increases in proportion to the square of its density, making denser regions stand out much more strongly.

More recently, astronomers observed gas in G2's trailing material gathering into another compact cloud that follows a similar orbit. Although this newly formed object might naturally be called G3, that designation had already been assigned to a different object. Together, the related clouds trace a connected flow of material through the Galactic Center, known as the G1-2-3 streamer.

Recent findings suggest that these clouds could play a surprisingly important role in sustaining the black hole. Calculations suggest that if approximately one Earth mass of gas reaches Sagittarius A* every ten years, it could provide enough fuel to maintain the black hole's current level of activity. Discovering how the clouds form could therefore help explain how the black hole receives its supply of matter.

Astronomers Trace the Gas Clouds to Their Source.

Researchers have considered several possible explanations for the clouds, including powerful winds from massive stars, stellar explosions such as novae, and gas pulled away from objects by the black hole's gravity.

Industry observers note that to investigate, the MPE-led team used two advanced infrared spectrographs, SINFONI and ERIS. Both instruments employ adaptive optics to produce sharper observations. By examining a specific hydrogen emission feature called the Brackett‑γ line, the astronomers measured the clouds' positions and velocities and reconstructed their paths around Sagittarius A*.

It has been revealed that the results revealed a striking pattern. G1, G2, and G2t all follow orbits with nearly the same shape and orientation. It would be extraordinarily unlikely for three unrelated clouds to share such closely matching orbital characteristics, strongly suggesting that they originated from the same source.

Two Massive Stars May Be Creating the Clouds.

By working backward from the clouds' observed motions and their velocities along our line of sight, the researchers identified a promising source: IRS 16SW, a massive contact binary system consisting of two stars in extremely close proximity.

The stellar pair belongs to a disk of young stars that revolves clockwise around Sagittarius A*. Its location and motion provide a plausible explanation for the gas stream. Even the slight differences between the clouds' orbital paths can be accounted for by the movement of the two stars around one another.

In a recent development, computer simulations of how gas flows and interacts provided additional support for this explanation. The models indicate that powerful stellar winds from the binary system can collide with surrounding material, creating a shock in the region between the stars. Gas then accumulates and becomes compressed, forming dense concentrations that can eventually separate from the system.

Sources indicate that once released, these compact clouds can travel inward along paths resembling those observed in the G1-2-3 streamer. This provides a physical explanation for how one binary star system could produce several distinct clouds moving along closely related orbits.

A Upcoming Clue to How Supermassive Black Holes Are Fed.

The findings suggest that massive stars near the Galactic Center may provide a continuing supply of gas capable of fueling Sagittarius A*. Rather than relying only on material already circulating around the black hole, the system could receive fresh gas from the powerful winds generated by nearby stars.

Sources indicate that the discovery also brings together several important processes in astronomy. The evolution of massive stars, the movement and compression of gas, and the supply of material to supermassive black holes may all be closely connected. By identifying a possible source of the mysterious clouds near Sagittarius A*, researchers have uncovered a new way in which stars could help sustain black hole activity at the heart of our own galaxy.

Walmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce growth ahead of the busy holiday season.

Walmart remarked global e-commerce sales surged 17% in the fiscal third quarter, driven by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, with Walmart U.S. up 23% and Sam's Club U.S. rising 30%. Its Walmart U.S. advertising business saw a 37% sales increase for the quarter.

Industry observers note that walmart said it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices.

CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the company has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices.

"The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner remarked in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can.".

CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that growth in online orders for Walmart and Sam's Club was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and reduced prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter.

"This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses.".

Sources indicate that walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to increase between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared with previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey said Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance.

Recent findings suggest that walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Recent findings suggest that for the quarter ended Oct. 31, the manufacturer reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 5.2%.

Adjusting for investment gains and losses, tax matters and reorganization charges, Walmart earned 65 cents per share.

Sources indicate that walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from a year earlier. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount.

Furner also mentioned Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average.

"It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he remarked.

Sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It remarked its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise.

In October, Walmart revealed it was launching a joint membership option with Walmart+ and Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer stand-alone memberships, as well.

Furner told CNBC the new membership has brought roughly 2 million new people into Sam's Club since its launch in late October. Though the company reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added that it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more.".

The company on Thursday said its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter.

It has been revealed that the tech giant is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter, the company remarked it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef.

Rainey remarked Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start.".

Recent findings suggest that the big-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.

Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U.S. space economy.

NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program recently selected 302 innovative projects, for a total investment of up to $171 million in seed funding.

In a recent development, this early-stage research and development work will tackle an array of topics, including those related to Artemis and the establishment of a U.S. Moon Base. Selected projects include next-generation battery solutions, robotic systems with sensing capabilities for the extreme lunar environment, and tools to prepare for construction of critical infrastructure, such as lunar landing pads.

Sources indicate that NASA’s SBIR/STTR program provides support for entrepreneurs, startups, and small businesses to advance and commercialize technologies that can advance the agency’s missions. Working with the program, a tech giant’s path toward commercialization or infusion into NASA missions occurs in phases. The latest awards involved two of these phases.

The newly introduced Phase I contracts will receive up to $225,000 each to establish the merit and feasibility of their proposed innovation. A portion of the projects selected are STTR awards, provided to small businesses partnered with research institutions.

The Phase II awards, with 98 contracts valued at up to $1.3 million each, will continue work begun in Phase I projects selected in 2025, targeting demonstration and delivery of the innovative technologies.

Following are a few examples of research supported through these recent awards:.

Sources indicate that an SBIR Phase II award for Opterus Research and Development Inc. supports a project focused on bringing power to the surface of the Moon and Mars by developing a modular system of rollable solar arrays. The arrays can be handled robotically, are compatible with various support structures, and work even in dusty surface conditions. The technology could be scaled up to 50 kilowatts, and it could provide a reliable power source to help both NASA and commercial space companies develop infrastructure on the Moon.

This SBIR Phase I award, led by Intelligent Fiber Optic Systems Corporation, aims to help lunar rovers perform complex tasks independently on the Moon. The firm’s 10-foot, extendable robotic arm can both “see” and has a sense of touch, combining a camera with sensors to detect and measure surface textures, contact forces, and temperature. The technology could help automate many lunar surface tasks, such as cleaning solar panels, positioning habitat structures, and collecting scientific samples from hard-to-reach locations. On Earth, the same instrumented robotic arms could be used to inspect and repair power lines, nuclear reactors, or other infrastructure in hazardous environments.

Elementium Materials Inc., selected for an SBIR Phase I award, is developing an ultra-cold-tolerant battery module for space applications and cold-climate uses on Earth. The technology can operate down to minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit without active heating, reducing the need for heaters and insulating layers to work on the Moon. With the space and mass that’s saved, NASA missions can launch other tools and science experiments, instead. This battery technology could help keep rovers, habitats, and other infrastructure running through the frigid, 14-day lunar night and potentially on Mars.

Industry observers note that A collaboration between Slate Geotechnical Consultants Inc. and the Colorado School of Mines will evaluate two approaches to preparing lunar regolith for repeated lunar landings, so that routine mission activities can have sturdy, reusable landing pads. Without such pads, the force generated by a rocket can blast out loose, gravel-like regolith from the surface, throw up dust, or create craters, potentially damaging spacecraft and nearby infrastructure. The project, supported by an STTR Phase I award, will also investigate ways to use rovers to repair and maintain future lunar landing pads.

Complete lists of the selected proposals are available on the SBIR/STTR program’s website: Phase I: 2026 NASA SBIR Appendix A Phase I 2026 NASA SBIR Appendix B Phase I 2026 NASA STTR Appendix B Phase I Phase II: 2025 NASA SBIR Phase II NASA’s SBIR/STTR program is part of the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate and is managed by NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data showed with all ballots counted.

“We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo said in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job.

According to recent reports, “We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister remarked in a speech to party members.

Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive latest leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash.

While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

According to recent reports, the NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

Orpo has mentioned he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

Industry observers note that the Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.

COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's looks to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.
  • But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.
  • "We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's looks to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

Recent findings suggest that "The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions.".

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

In a recent development, the European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report covers climate protection and impact.

Recent findings suggest that "It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," stated a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Recent findings suggest that disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," mentioned a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have remarked the timeline is attainable.

"We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive.".

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake.".

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra remarked it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science.".

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

It has been revealed that the IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the intends to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

At least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment.".

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

Repression against Iranian lawyers increases

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • UN human rights experts have called on the Iranian authorities to end the escalating persecution of independent lawyers.
  • "Independent lawyers are increasingly being prosecuted and intimidated for their professional work and for defending human rights," the experts mentioned in a statement in mid-November.
  • Recent findings suggest that they said that between September 2025 and September 2026, at least 135 lawyers were issued with a summons, arrested, detained, suspended, dismissed or banned from traveling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UN human rights experts have called on the Iranian authorities to end the escalating persecution of independent lawyers. They warn that limiting access to legal representation increases the risk of arbitrary detention, coerced confessions and unfair trials.

"Independent lawyers are increasingly being prosecuted and intimidated for their professional work and for defending human rights," the experts mentioned in a statement in mid-November.

Recent findings suggest that they said that between September 2025 and September 2026, at least 135 lawyers were issued with a summons, arrested, detained, suspended, dismissed or banned from traveling. In January and February 2026, 23 lawyers, including five women, were reportedly arrested after nationwide protests.

It has been revealed that A current example is the case of Amirsalar Davoudi, a human rights lawyer who was arrested in October in the central Iranian city of Isfahan, where he was defending a client in the Revolutionary Court. According to Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), he was taken to hospital on November 9 after suffering a heart attack in custody.

"There is a long history to the persecution of and coercive measures taken against lawyers," Sina Yousefi, a 41-year-old lawyer and human rights activist, told DW.

It has been revealed that in October 2022, Yousefi was arrested by security forces in Tabriz during the nationwide "Woman Life Freedom" protests. Later, he was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for "propaganda against the system." He has since left Iran, and now lives in the German capital Berlin.

According to recent reports, "The pressure was already increasing on lawyers back then, because they were undertaking the defense of people who were arrested and publicly expressing their support for the demonstrators," noted Yousefi. "The security services, judiciary, and criminal prosecution apparatus increasingly used targeted mechanisms to move against independent lawyers.".

In a recent development, even renowned and internationally known lawyers such as Nasrin Sotoudeh, who was co-awarded the Sakharov Prize in 2012, have been affected by this repression. In 2026, Sotoudeh was awarded the Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prizeafter being repeatedly arrested and imprisoned.

Industry observers note that yousefi said arrests and threats against lawyers working on political and human rights cases not only curtailed the rights of those accused to a defense, but also discouraged other lawyers from accepting such briefs. This, he added, compromised the fairness of trials.

Recent findings suggest that criminal proceedings have also been instigated, or other measures taken, against lawyers who undertook to represent demonstrators. Comments on social media about the violation of civil rights can also be cited as grounds for investigation and judicial proceedings.

Sources indicate that yousefi also warned against tightening restrictions on a person's right to choose their own lawyer. According to the note to Article 48 of Iran's Code of Criminal Procedure, for people arrested on certain charges, access to lawyers of their own choosing is already restricted during the investigation phase. Defendants must resort to lawyers approved by the head of the judiciary. In some cases, even these lawyers are not granted access to all the files and evidence.

According to Yousefi, in many cases in which charges have been brought against demonstrators, lawyers have only been granted access to the files "when the preliminary investigations have been concluded and the evidence for the prosecution has been gathered — including confessions made during their imprisonment." Even then, he stated, "their access to the records is limited and they have little time to prepare the defense.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"In many cases," Yousefi added, "the judges ascribe greater importance to reports by security agents than to the defense. Verdicts are handed down predominantly on the basis of this.".

Industry observers note that shabnam Moinipour, the program director at the Center for Supporters of Human Rights (CSHR) in the UK, sees the independence of the bar as a fundamental precondition for the effective defense of citizens. The organization monitors the situation of lawyers in Iran, documenting violations of their rights, and following up at an international level.

"A lawyer must be able to call into question the charges brought by the public prosecutor and the credibility of the security agencies' reports without fear of criminal prosecution," Moinipour told DW. "Because when a lawyer's freedom and professional activity are threatened, their client's right to defense is impaired.".

In Moinipour's view, when the decision as to which lawyers are approved is made by the most senior representative of the same court authority, it raises serious questions about the independence of the bar.

According to recent reports, "This restriction has psychological as well as legal consequences," she stressed. "For the accused, it may reinforce a sense of being unprotected, as well as feelings of fear and mistrust. It can also prevent them from disclosing details of threats, torture, and illegal behavior.".

Moinipour considers this practice incompatible with Iran's obligations as a member of the UN Human Rights Committee. International law stipulates that people must have immediate access to a lawyer of their own choosing, be able to communicate with them in confidence and be supplied with sufficient means to mount a defense.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that referring to a joint report by the Tehran-based Defenders of Human Rights Center and the International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute (IBAHRI), as well as the recent statement by UN human rights experts, Moinipour said: "Even without mass arrests, the actions taken against a limited number of lawyers can send a threatening message to others and restrict their professional activity. This phenomenon is described as a chilling or deterrent effect.".

Recent findings suggest that however, Moinipour stressed that, despite this pressure, "many lawyers in Iran continue to defend the rights of their clients and accept the risk of arrest, criminal prosecution, and professional restrictions. In doing so, they are prepared, if necessary, to pay a high price for this resistance.".

#81945. After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1625 w)

After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that after eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object.
  • In a recent development, scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission.
  • It has been revealed that the telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object. The instrument, built in the UK, successfully detected X-rays from the Crab Nebula, one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, marking an vital milestone for the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's BepiColombo mission.

In a recent development, scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission. Their initial results are highly encouraging, arriving just as BepiColombo prepares to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21.

It has been revealed that the telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly. Although engineers monitored MIXS throughout the journey, the instrument could not look directly into space until September. That opportunity came after the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the two science orbiters, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) or Mio.

With its view finally unobstructed, MIXS could begin the critical tests needed before the spacecraft enters its planned orbit around the solar system's smallest planet.

A Telescope's First Look Across 6,500 Light-Years.

Industry observers note that for its first astronomical target, the team selected the Crab Nebula, located approximately 6,500 light-years from Earth. This well-studied remnant of an exploded star produces a strong, predictable X-ray signal, making it an ideal reference for testing the telescope's performance.

In a recent development, by examining how MIXS observes this distant object, researchers can determine whether the instrument still performs as expected after its lengthy journey. They can also compare the results with laboratory measurements collected in 2015, when the telescope was last tested on Earth.

The main observation campaign took place on September 11 and 12. Over 39 hours, the spacecraft carried out 55 carefully controlled changes in orientation to collect the data.

Industry observers note that one vital measurement was the telescope's angular resolution, which describes its ability to distinguish small details in an image. Scientists determined this by examining how widely the Crab Nebula's X-ray signal spread across the detector. Remarkably, MIXS delivered slightly sharper resolution than it had during its laboratory tests in 2015.

That improvement is particularly encouraging because the instrument will eventually use its X-ray vision to investigate the composition of Mercury's surface.

Better Than Expected After Eight Years in Space.

Professor Emma Bunce, Principal Investigator (PI) for MIXS and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester, welcomed the results as a major achievement for the international team responsible for developing the instrument.

Professor Bunce remarked: "We have waited a long time to make measurements with MIXS and it is fantastic to see it operating brilliantly in space. This is testament to our engineering and technical team, and our international partners who we have worked with over many years to build this incredible instrument. 80% of the technology on MIXS is new!

According to recent reports, "During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out. We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the Sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after 8 years in space.

"We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase.".

The results suggest that the telescope has weathered its long exposure to the harsh space environment exceptionally well. Engineers have found no unwanted visible light interfering with its images, and the effects of high-energy cosmic rays are understood well enough to be removed during data processing.

Recent findings suggest that the team has also identified a small amount of X-ray emission originating within the instrument itself when sunlight strikes its optics. However, this effect is not expected to interfere with observations of Mercury's sunlit surface. Most importantly, the detector shows no signs of radiation damage after eight years in space.

Some remaining effects still require investigation, and scientists expect to make further adjustments after the spacecraft reaches Mercury to ensure that MIXS is ready for its full scientific mission.

How X-Rays Will Reveal Mercury's Hidden Chemistry.

Industry observers note that bepiColombo is designed to investigate Mercury in unprecedented detail. As the smallest and one of the least explored rocky planets in our solar system, Mercury offers scientists a rare opportunity to understand how planets form and change under the extreme conditions found close to a star.

In a recent development, one of the mission's major goals is to uncover the planet's chemical composition and geological history. These findings could help explain Mercury's unusual characteristics while providing broader insights into the formation and evolution of the solar system.

According to recent reports, MIXS, carried aboard the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), will play a central role in this investigation. Developed by a European consortium led by the University of Leicester, it draws on the university's long history of X-ray astronomy research.

It is the first imaging X-ray telescope to operate on a planetary science mission. Working alongside other scientific instruments, MIXS will help produce a global map showing the elements that make up Mercury's surface, revealing its atomic composition in greater detail than ever before. It is also the only UK-led scientific instrument aboard BepiColombo and receives support from the UK Space Agency.

The instrument works by detecting fluorescent X-rays released by rocks on Mercury's surface. When powerful X-rays from the Sun strike these rocks, they can cause atoms within the material to emit X-rays of their own. Different elements produce characteristic X-ray signals, allowing scientists to identify what the surface is made of without collecting physical samples.

MIXS will make these measurements with assistance from the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), which monitors the solar radiation and particles reaching Mercury.

According to recent reports, the telescope will also examine X-rays emitted from Mercury's nighttime surface when charged particles associated with the planet's magnetic environment strike it. These measurements could reveal crucial connections between Mercury's surface and the surrounding space environment.

A 10 Billion Kilometer Journey With a Personal Legacy.

Sources indicate that for Dr. Adrian Martindale, MIXS Instrument Scientist at the University of Leicester's School of Physics and Astronomy, the successful observations represent the culmination of more than two decades of work.

Martindale joined the project in 2003 while still an undergraduate student and has been involved in nearly every aspect of the instrument's development.

Dr. Martindale remarked: "BepiColombo, and MIXS in particular, are like part of my family. I've been involved since I was an undergraduate and touched almost every part of the instrument before it was debuted.

"This first data is mind-blowing to me. The last time we could see through this telescope it was in the basement under the School of Physics and Astronomy in Leicester, but after a rocket launch, eight years in space and 10 billion kilometers traveled it looks just the same. I can't wait to see the science data it produces when we get into orbit.".

The milestone also carries special meaning for the team because MIXS represents the scientific legacy of Professor George Fraser. Fraser was the instrument's original Principal Investigator and the driving force behind its innovative optical design before his death in March 2014.

Professor Bunce added: "We are thinking of George as we operate MIXS fully in space for the first time and know that he would be very, very proud of the team and delighted at our first light observations.".

BepiColombo Prepares for Its Final Arrival at Mercury.

BepiColombo began its arrival phase on September 3, when the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the spacecraft assembly.

In a recent development, the remaining connected spacecraft are scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21. The two science orbiters, MPO and Mio, are then expected to separate on December 9 to 10, allowing them to prepare for their respective scientific operations.

It has been revealed that the mission's primary science phase is scheduled to begin in April 2027. Once underway, BepiColombo will investigate Mercury's surface, internal structure, magnetic field, and surrounding environment, helping scientists piece together the history of a planet that remains surprisingly mysterious despite its proximity to the Sun.

For the MIXS team, the successful first observations of the Crab Nebula offer an early indication of what the instrument may accomplish when it finally turns its attention to Mercury.

International Collaboration and Funding.

MIXS was developed through a partnership involving research institutions and technology companies across Europe. Participating organizations include:.

UK funding for the BepiColombo MIXS instrument comes from the UK Space Agency, which serves as the lead funding organization, along with STFC, the European Space Agency, and the University of Leicester.

Britain's pound is beating every other major currency this year

📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget intends by former Prime Minister Liz Truss.
  • Industry observers note that sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022.
  • Recent findings suggest that the UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget intends by former Prime Minister Liz Truss. Now, it’s enjoying a comeback.

Industry observers note that sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022. The pound, which has advanced about 3.3% versus the greenback since the start of 2023, is the best-performing currency among developed economies this year.

Recent findings suggest that the UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected. Activity is now thought to have expanded 0.1% in the final three months of last year, up from a previous estimate of no growth at all. Gross domestic product growth in January has been estimated at 0.3% after dropping 0.5% in December.

In a recent development, this resilience is bolstering expectations the Bank of England will maintain aggressive interest rate hikes despite concerns about the health of the global banking sector. Rising rates can boost the domestic currency because they help attract foreign investors searching for higher returns.

Inflation in the United Kingdom also jumped to an annual rate of 10.4% in February, underscoring the need for the Bank of England to maintain its tough approach.

The pound plunged close to $1.03 in September 2022 after the Truss government unveiled plans to boost borrowing while slashing taxes, unleashing panic in financial markets that fueled fears of a recession in the United Kingdom.

The International Monetary Fund predicted in January that the UK economy would contract by 0.6% this year, while all other advanced economies would grow, if only slightly.

“There was a lot of pessimism being priced into the pound,” said Francesco Pesole, a currency strategist at ING.

But the sharp pullback in energy prices and China’s reopening have provided some relief about the economic outlook since the start of the year.

“There was a substantial re-rating of growth expectations around Europe, and that impacted the UK,” Pesole said.

The euro has also been lifted by these dynamics, rising 2.3% against the US dollar in 2023. The pound’s rally has been sharper in large part because its 2022 declines were more severe, according to Pesole.

Both currencies have been aided by the greenback’s sharp drop from highs reached last September as recession fears have percolated in the United States.

A lack of clarity around the Federal Reserve’s next steps has also restrained the dollar in recent weeks. Investor speculation has increased that the Fed could pause or stop rate hikes due to concerns about the economy following the failure of Silicon Valley Bank last month.

Recent findings suggest that jordan Rochester, a currency strategist at Nomura, noted he thinks the pound could rise to $1.30 this year and “potentially higher.” But he still sees risks given the uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England’s prepares and how rate rises will feed back through the country’s economy. And Pesole cautioned that currency fluctuations are often overdone when markets are choppy, as they are now.

“In a volatile market environment, moves are exacerbated,” he noted.

Your teen wants to play GTA 6. Heres what to know.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that grand Theft Auto VI fans waited more than a decade for a fresh installment of the best-selling video game of all time.
  • Now they've grown up and they're itching to not just play GTA 6; they're also eager to participate in the Grand Theft Auto discourse.
  • From the debate over killing or sparing a character named Arnold to cataloguing all the wildlife cameos to the game's hot soundtrack, GTA 6 is driving countless conversations amongst players, including teens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that grand Theft Auto VI fans waited more than a decade for a fresh installment of the best-selling video game of all time. That includes teens who were toddlers when the game's last chapter debuted.

Now they've grown up and they're itching to not just play GTA 6; they're also eager to participate in the Grand Theft Auto discourse.

From the debate over killing or sparing a character named Arnold to cataloguing all the wildlife cameos to the game's hot soundtrack, GTA 6 is driving countless conversations amongst players, including teens.

In a recent development, but the game is rated 17+ and features adult content, including sex, strip clubs, drugs, graphic violence, and murder. So, many parents whose teens want to play GTA 6 will likely find themselves in the familiar yet tricky position of balancing their child's interests and social life with exposure to content they feel violates their family's values.

Dr. Brett Biller, a child psychologist at Hackensack University Medical Center, wants parents to know it's OK — even advisable, in his opinion — to say no to GTA 6.

Biller has no problem with video games in general. In fact, he acknowledges how online interactive games can have benefits, like socializing with friends over play.

Ultimately, however, he believes exposing tweens and teens to GTA 6's hyperrealistic community violence is simply not worth it.

"The negative consequences can outweigh the positive impact," Biller says.

Sources indicate that while research doesn't prove that video game violence causes aggressive behavior, Biller notes there's a correlation between between violence in the home and aggression. That makes Biller cautious about exposing kids and teens to violent video games.

Industry observers note that killing zombies, he notes, is much different than murdering human characters, and younger children don't consistently grasp the difference between fantasy and reality. Yet Biller states older teens can also struggle in this way, especially given the realism of GTA 6. Plus, the game may normalize community violence by putting a teen player in the shoes of a thief or killer.

Meanwhile, teens with a history of witnessing or experiencing violence who play GTA 6 may find it difficult to manage the game's stimuli and their feelings about the content, Biller adds.

Beyond concerns about violence, parents may say no because they understand how playing GTA 6 will affect their child's mood, sleep, and personality.

"We, as caregivers, are responsible for making decisions that are in the best interest of our children," Biller says.

He recommends parents who won't permit their teen to play GTA 6 validate their child's frustration or fears of being left out.

Parents can also model how peer pressure is real and hard, because they feel it when other adults let their teen play GTA 6.

Biller says this conversation presents a good opportunity to help a teen understand that standing up for their principles isn't always easy. He suggests parents explore with their teen other activities they can do with friends instead of playing GTA 6.

While some parents might feel better about playing alongside their teen, instead of the teen playing with friends, Biller says this approach is a "double-edged sword" that requires care and vigilance.

In a recent development, on one hand, parents who co-play have ample chances to point out and discuss concerning content or themes with their teen. On the other, co-playing can model to a teen that violence is fun or not a big deal.

In more cases than not, Biller finds that parents use this approach when they don't feel confident saying no or to justify their own choices.

Common Sense Media, a nonprofit organization that reviews and rates entertainment content, described GTA 6 as an "extremely mature crime game" for adults 18 and older.

Industry observers note that still, its review notes that only parents will know if their older teen is ready to play. Either way, Jasmine Hood Miller, director of family resources and content strategy for Common Sense Media, indicates parents should talk to their teen about the game.

Topics for discussion can include what looks fun about GTA 6, how women are depicted in sex scenes and strip clubs, and whether they think they'd hurt people in the game, or have done so.

"It can be uncomfortable to talk about some of those topics," Miller notes. "But honestly, if your kid is not talking to you, they're talking to someone else.".

Miller adds that these conversations should feel low pressure and not like a lecture. Instead, Miller encourages parents to be curious and nonjudgemental.

If a teen plays or watches the game at a friend's house, even after their parent has mentioned no, Biller recommends better understanding the context and validating their teen's feelings.

In a recent development, "Reward them for being honest," he indicates. "We want them to continue to be open with us." It has been revealed that gap Inc. on Thursday confirmed Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.

The retailer also stated Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday.

Recent findings suggest that kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that.

Sources indicate that "I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement.

The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.

In a recent development, "Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode.".

In a recent development, dickson stated the organization is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.

While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson said this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential.

Gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount.

In a recent development, net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%.

Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.

The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share.

Dickson remarked in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season.

"We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson remarked.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Recent findings suggest that for the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior.

At Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the organization attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. `.

The firm's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson remarked it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales.

"Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson noted.

Sources indicate that the Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its new CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2.

In a recent development, banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the company attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.

Dickson stated the brand has since introduced latest products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country.

"We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth.".

#81937. NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1628 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1628 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.
  • In a recent development, the historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m.
  • The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. After more than 49 years of traveling through space, humanity's most distant spacecraft is now approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from home. At that distance, even a signal moving at the speed of light needs an entire day to make the journey.

In a recent development, the historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST). Scientists and engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, received a signal from Voyager 1 early Thursday, exactly 24 hours after the spacecraft reached the milestone.

The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.

Voyager 1 Is Now 24 Light-Hours From Earth.

Industry observers note that astronomers often describe enormous cosmic distances in terms of how long light takes to travel them. A light-day represents the distance light covers in 24 hours, or roughly 16.1 billion miles.

In a recent development, light moves through a vacuum at approximately 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) per second. To put Voyager 1's distance in perspective, sunlight passing Earth takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon. Reaching Neptune takes roughly four hours, while traveling from Neptune to Voyager 1 requires another 20 hours.

Even these enormous distances are small compared with those separating stars. A single light-year, the distance light travels in one year, measures approximately 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

Voyager 1's extraordinary distance also creates a major challenge for mission controllers. Sending a command to the spacecraft now requires 24 hours, and receiving a response takes another 24 hours. A complete exchange therefore spans two full days, even though the signals travel at the fastest speed possible.

The milestone comes as engineers investigate a communication problem. NASA has not received scientific or engineering data from Voyager 1 since November 14. However, the probe continues transmitting a carrier signal, the radio signal that normally carries information back to Earth. By tracking this signal and calculating the spacecraft's trajectory, mission specialists were able to verify that Voyager 1 had crossed the one light-day mark. Engineers are continuing to investigate why the expected data is not coming through.

A Historic Journey Beyond the Solar System's Planets.

Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, were debuted in 1977 to take advantage of an unusual arrangement of the outer planets. The alignment allowed the spacecraft to use planetary gravity to travel from one destination to another, making an ambitious exploration mission possible.

Sources indicate that managed by JPL, the Voyagers became the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn. They also delivered the first high-resolution images of these distant planets, revealing extraordinary fresh details about their atmospheres, rings, and moons. Voyager 2 continued farther, becoming the first spacecraft to explore Uranus and Neptune up close.

Today, both probes are traveling through interstellar space, making them humanity's only spacecraft to have crossed into the region beyond the Sun's protective bubble. Their instruments continue monitoring changes in the Sun's magnetic field across immense distances, providing scientists with measurements that cannot be collected from Earth.

"Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets," said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. "But it went on to become central to NASA's fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.".

"Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery," noted Dave Gallagher, JPL director. "Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.".

Voyager's Golden Record Carries a Message From Earth.

The Voyager spacecraft carry more than scientific instruments. Each also holds a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing images and sounds representing life on Earth. These recordings were designed as messages that an advanced extraterrestrial civilization might discover someday.

According to recent reports, the records give the mission a purpose extending far beyond its scientific discoveries. Even after the spacecraft eventually lose the ability to communicate with Earth, they will continue traveling through space with a small collection of sights and sounds from the planet that launched them.

"Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward," said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. "Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.".

Exploring the Mysterious Region Beyond the Sun.

In a recent development, voyager 1 is currently moving through space at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph). In 2012, it became the first spacecraft to cross the boundary of the heliosphere, a vast region surrounding the Sun that is filled with particles and magnetic fields generated by our star.

This protective bubble helps shield the solar system from cosmic radiation arriving from elsewhere in the galaxy. Beyond its outer boundary lies interstellar space, where particles and magnetic fields from the broader galaxy become more dominant.

Voyager 2 followed a different route and crossed into interstellar space in 2018. Together, the probes are providing the first direct observations of conditions beyond the heliosphere.

Sources indicate that one of their most intriguing discoveries is that the Sun's effects do not simply disappear at the boundary. Its influence appears to extend much farther into interstellar space than scientists once understood, raising new questions about where the environment shaped by our star truly gives way to the surrounding galaxy.

"The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere," said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. "One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.".

How NASA Is Keeping Voyager 1 Alive After Nearly 50 Years.

Operating spacecraft built nearly half a century ago requires increasingly inventive engineering. Both Voyagers have experienced problems as their equipment ages, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer. NASA engineers have repeatedly developed solutions that allow the probes to continue working despite these setbacks.

Electricity has become one of the mission's greatest limitations. Earlier in 2026, engineers took a calculated risk by switching off three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replacing them with three alternatives that consume less power. This change was intended to help the spacecraft stretch its remaining energy supply.

It has been revealed that voyager 1 depends on a radioisotope thermal generator that is now approximately 50 years old. Often described as a nuclear battery, the device produces electricity by converting heat released during the radioactive decay of plutonium.

As the radioactive material continues to decay, the available power gradually decreases. Both Voyager spacecraft lose approximately four watts of electrical output every year, forcing engineers to make difficult decisions about which systems can remain operational.

The latest conservation measures are expected to provide enough power to operate the spacecraft's current scientific instruments until at least the summer of 2027, when both probes will celebrate their 50th launch anniversaries.

One Day, Voyager 1 Will Become a Silent Messenger to the Stars.

In a recent development, maintaining contact across such staggering distances requires some of NASA's most powerful communications equipment. The agency relies on its Deep Space Network, a worldwide system of large radio antennas located at three facilities, to communicate with Voyager and other spacecraft traveling to and beyond the Moon.

Despite the enormous communication delay and the spacecraft's aging systems, engineers continue monitoring Voyager 1 daily and transmitting instructions every week. The mission remains an extraordinary demonstration of what long-term spacecraft engineering can achieve.

"We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to," said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. "Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity's silent ambassador to the stars.".
